title: ‘Concerning’ low sea ice persists as Antarctic hits third-lowest winter peak - Carbon Brief
gist: Provisional NSIDC data show Antarctic sea ice hit its third-smallest winter peak (17.59m km2 on 14 September 2026), extending a run of record-low winters since 2022-23, while the Arctic minimum (4.60m km2 on 12 September) tied for 10th-lowest despite cool, cloudy weather in the Pacific sector. Scientists say it is too early to call a structural shift in Antarctica, and warn that NOAA's March 2026 termination of an air-pressure dataset has halted the PIOMAS Arctic ice-thickness record. (Note: the chart captions in the text appear swapped between Arctic and Antarctic.)

insights.claim: Antarctic sea ice reached its 2026 winter peak on 14 September at 17.59m km2, the third-smallest maximum in the 48-year satellite record, per provisional NSIDC data.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Adds a fourth consecutive-ish low winter to the Antarctic record, reinforcing the case that Southern Ocean conditions have shifted since 2023.

insights.claim: All five of the lowest July Antarctic sea ice extents on record have occurred since 2022 and all four of the lowest August extents since 2023; July and August 2026 ranked fifth and fourth lowest respectively.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Clustering of record lows in recent years is the key signal that a regime change may be under way rather than random variability.

insights.claim: After several decades of stable or increasing winter Antarctic sea ice, scientists cannot yet attribute the persistent recent lows to human-caused warming versus natural variability, and more years of data are needed to confirm a structural shift.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Attribution uncertainty means Antarctic sea-ice trends remain a watch item rather than settled science for climate-risk models.
insights.quote: We need more years of observations to better understand whether this is truly a structural shift.

insights.claim: Antarctic sea ice went from a near-average February 2026 minimum back to unusually low winter coverage, showing that summer-season normality does not predict winter recovery.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Seasonal readings can mislead; winter maxima are the more telling metric for the Antarctic trend.

insights.claim: Regional Antarctic ice patterns flipped during the 2026 growth season: the Bellingshausen Sea was almost ice-free in April while the Amundsen Sea had excess ice, but by late August pressure and wind changes had largely erased the Bellingshausen deficit and left the Amundsen Sea and much of East Antarctica unusually ice-scarce.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: Atmospheric circulation drives large regional swings, so single-region anomalies should not be extrapolated to the whole continent.

insights.claim: Arctic sea ice in March 2026 reached a winter peak that was joint-smallest in the nearly 50-year satellite record, meaning 2026 combined a record-low winter maximum with a mid-ranked summer minimum.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon

insights.claim: In March 2026 NOAA terminated a global air-pressure dataset that underpinned the PIOMAS Arctic ice-thickness reanalysis (running since 1979), forcing both to stop publishing updates, with PIOMAS unsure whether funding allows it to resume.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: US federal cuts to climate datasets degrade observational continuity that climate-risk, insurance and research users depend on; expect gaps in thickness-based Arctic monitoring.

insights.claim: Scientists say ice extent alone is insufficient and more observations of metrics such as ice thickness are needed to gauge the overall condition of the Arctic ice pack, especially in fragmented years like 2026, precisely as the main thickness record has been suspended.
insights.speaker: Ayesha Tandon
insights.so_what: The monitoring gap raises uncertainty around Arctic ice condition; alternative (e.g. non-US or private) data providers may gain relevance.
